title: Evanescent-wave Johnson Noise from Superconductors
authors: Hruday Mallubhotla, Gustav Romare, Ilya Esterlis, Maxim Vavilov, Robert Joynt, Alex Levchenko
abstract: We compute the evanescent-wave Johnson noise (EWJN) in the vacuum half-space above a superconductor, and the resulting relaxation time ($T_1$) of spin and charge qubits placed at nanometer distances from the surface. The electromagnetic response is described by a single microscopic transverse current-response kernel $Q(q, ω)$ for a BCS superconductor. This is computed for varying densities of both non-magnetic impurities and magnetic impurities, for arbitrary frequency and temperature and for wave vectors $q \ll k_F$ (the Fermi wavevector). When combined with the fluctuation-dissipation theorem and the nonlocal surface impedances of the half-space, this yields the magnetic and electric field noise at any distance $z \gg k_F^{-1}$ from the surface, from which we obtain $T_1$. Just below $T_c$ the magnetic noise is enhanced relative to the normal state by the coherence (Hebel-Slichter-type) peak of the dissipative conductivity and drops exponentially at lower temperatures; the electric noise shows no coherence peak. The theory predicts that there is a zero-temperature noise floor induced by magnetic impurities. In the gapless regime produced by pair breaking, the finite subgap density of states $ν(0)$ yields a temperature-independent noise spectral density and a relaxation rate bounded by $T_1^{-1}(T)\le[ν(0)/ν_F]^{2}\,T_{1,N}^{-1}(T)$ for $T\ll T_c$, with equality in the extreme nonlocal regime. Here $ν(0)$ and $ν_F$ are the superconducting and normal-state densities of states at the Fermi energy, and $T_{1,N}(T)$ is the relaxation time the same electrode would produce in its normal state at the same temperature.
summary: This theoretical paper calculates the Johnson noise emitted by superconductors in the near-field vacuum, quantifying how this noise limits the coherence time ($T_1$) of nearby qubits. Key findings include the prediction of a coherence-enhanced noise peak below $T_c$ and the establishment of a temperature-independent noise floor due to magnetic impurities in the gapless regime.
main_problem: The paper computes the evanescent-wave Johnson noise (EWJN) generated by superconductors and determines its effect on the relaxation time ($T_1$) of nearby quantum qubits.
main_result: The magnetic noise exhibits a Hebel-Slichter-type coherence peak below $T_c$, and the theory predicts a zero-temperature noise floor induced by magnetic impurities in the gapless regime.
method: The analysis uses the fluctuation-dissipation theorem applied to the electromagnetic response, deriving the noise kernels from the microscopic transverse current-response kernel $Q(q, \omega)$.
model_or_system: The system involves a qubit placed in vacuum above a bulk BCS superconductor. The theory incorporates impurity scattering (non-magnetic and magnetic) and analyzes the response in the near-field (evanescent wave) regime.
key_observables: Relaxation rate ($1/T_1$) of spin and charge qubits; magnetic and electric field noise spectral densities ($b_B, b_E$).

main_assumptions: The formalism assumes the near-field approximation ($z \ll c/\omega$) and uses the quasiclassical (Fermi-surface) approximation for response functions.

paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by calculating the microscopic transverse current-response kernel, applying the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, and deriving the final $T_1$ expression, analyzing different temperature and impurity regimes.
why_interesting: This work directly connects superconducting electrodynamics (Johnson noise) to open quantum system dynamics ($T_1$ relaxation), providing quantitative predictions for decoherence mechanisms in solid-state quantum devices.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A qubit with level splitting ℏω0 in vacuum, placed a distance z above a metal which becomes a supercon- ductor at low temperatures. Current fluctuations in the metal/superconductor generate evanescent electromagnetic waves that relax the qubit with the rate 1/T1.
FIG. 2. Quasiparticle density of states from the Shiba theory, Eqs. (31)–(33), for representative parameters (cf. Ref. [43], Fig. 1). Energies are measured in units of the self-consistent gap ∆.
FIG. 3. Self-consistent gap with magnetic pair breaking, from Eqs. (35)–(36). The dashed curve is the near-Tc formula, shown to emphasize its limited domain of validity.

FIG. 4. Transverse dielectric function of Nb at 2.88 GHz, for the superconducting (blue) vs. normal (red) states. Solid lines are for clean samples (τTc = 20, ℓ= 4.2 µm, 1/ℓ= 2.4 × 105 m−1) and dashed lines are for dirty samples (τTc = 0.02, ℓ= 4.2 nm, 1/ℓ= 2.4 × 108 m−1). 1/ξ0 = 2.6 × 107 m−1. Three temperatures are shown. The plotted range 105 m−1 ≤q ≤ 109 m−1 corresponds to the dominant momenta q ∼1/2z for qubit heights between ∼1 nm and several micrometers, i.e., the experimentally relevant range; the upper end is still an order of magnitude below kF , where the quasiclassical kernel applies.

FIG. 5. Dirty-limit σ1(T)/σn at 2.88 GHz as computed from the kernel (43), for τTc = 0.02 (1/τ ≈28 ∆0); in this k →0, 1/τ ≫∆limit the ratio σ1/σn is independent of τ (Mattis– Bardeen) and of the material parameters other than ∆(T). As magnetic scattering is turned on the coherence peak disap- pears and the system becomes gapless. In the gapless regime the residual dissipation satisfies σ1(0)/σn = [ν(0)/νF]2.
